chapter_theme: The one song at Thiruvallam (திருவல்லம்): the body as a walking hut of skin, flesh and bone, and a plea for the strength to proclaim Murugan before the devotees before the senses carry the life away.

665.reading: The poet pictures the body as a hut of desire and skin, flesh and fluids, with bones driven in as pegs, walking on two legs, and asks that, lest the life, like a fierce elephant, run loose along the paths of the senses when its time of speed comes, Murugan give him the strength to recite 'Vel, Kanda' faultlessly before the devotees who fall at his feet. The praise names Vishnu who played the flute and who came before an eyelid could blink when the elephant, in distress, cried 'Moolam, rule me', and Thiruvallam, Siva's ancient town round which Brahma, the directions, earth and sky revolve, where women come to dance.
665.nuance: The body is a hut (குடில்) built of skin, flesh, water and bone pegs (என்புறு கீல்), a builder's inventory of the body. The life as an elephant on the paths of the senses is answered in the praise by Gajendra, the elephant saved when it called. The plea is for speech, the strength (விறல்) to praise aloud among devotees.

links.note: Both take the body apart into its stuff, skin, flesh, blood and bone: the Naladiyar to ask which part is the desired woman, 665 to show the hut the life lives in before it asks for the strength to praise.

665 fears that when its time of speed comes the life, like a fierce elephant (வெங்கனல் உயிர் வேழம்), will run loose along the paths of the senses. The Kural praises one who guards the five senses with the goad of firmness (உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்), the goad implying the senses as elephants. The Kural answers with firmness; the song asks instead for the strength to recite 'Vel, Kanda'.

source_issues: Song 665: one corrupt character in குடிலு஡டே (line 546), probably குடிலூடே.
